slices.behaviour: F19: a relation in public that is not a table cannot be born reachable. Part 6 revokes the default privileges for role postgres, strips any non-table relation of client-bound privileges, and raises on a view without security_invoker or on any materialised view in public; part 4's revoke loop and self-check now read all five row-bearing kinds.
slices.failure_reason: `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` exited 1: "A view over public.shipments, which holds buyer name and buyer address, handed another tenant's buyer data to 2 of the 2 roles a browser request is bound to, while the same roles are refused the table itself", and "16 default privileges stand on schema public, so every table, view and materialised view a later migration creates there is born holding them".

slices.behaviour: F20: every column that can hold a sentence is classified rather than matched by name. Part 7 carries 114 column comments; nine columns are buyer PII, including claims.claim_text, messages.body and message_threads.subject, and 111 say why a buyer's name and address cannot reach them.
slices.failure_reason: `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` exited 1: "114 of the 120 columns in schema public that can hold a sentence say neither that they hold buyer data nor why a buyer's name and address cannot reach them, so SEEN-083 cannot know which of them it has to expire", naming every candidate, so it could not be cleared by adding three names to a list.

slices.behaviour: F21: an erased tenant id is spent. Part 8 adds seen.erased_tenants, a tombstone of tenant_id and erased_at and nothing else, written after a delete on public.tenants, with an insert carrying a tombstoned id refused and the registry itself append-only for every role including the owner.
slices.failure_reason: `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` exited 1: "An erased tenant id was inserted again, leaving 1 tenant row standing with 0 audit events behind it, so the erasure of that tenant is indistinguishable from no erasure having happened, where a refusal (23001) is what keeps the id spent and the erasure legible".

slices.behaviour: F23 and F22: the append-only exception asks whether the tenant is gone rather than whether it is visible, seen.refuse_audit_mutation now being security definer; and the stated reason for the eight column-list set-null keys is corrected to the one that reproduces, the ordinary parent-row delete.
slices.failure_reason: `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` exited 1: "A role a request can be bound to asked to delete an audit event of a tenant that is there, carrying that tenant's own claim, and the database answered accepted, leaving 0 audit events. The caller could see 0 of the 1 tenant rows that exist, so an exception branch that reads invisibility as absence stood open."

slices.behaviour: F24: why a restricting key is excluded is corrected in all four places that carried the claim, to the ordinary parent-row delete rather than a tenant's erasure, with a new test measuring what a restricting key actually does. Excluding restrict is unchanged and still enforced.
slices.failure_reason: `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` exited 1 with the claim encoded as behaviour rather than matched as text: "With `on delete restrict` in place of the key a claim is credited by, deleting the settlement line answered 23503 and erasing the tenant answered accepted", against an expected 23503.

slices.behaviour: F25: the suite runs its test files one at a time, because they share one database, and the fixtures that erased a tenant now roll back so they leave no tombstone. fileParallelism is false with the hazard named in a comment.
slices.failure_reason: `pnpm --filter @seen/core test` exited 1 with 5 of 6 files failing: the configuration assertion, "runs its test files one at a time, because they share one database: expected undefined to be false", and eight afterAll failures of the form "Tenants this file created are tombstoned in the erasure registry, so its fixtures erased them outside a transaction and nothing can take those rows back".
